```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5.6, dpi = 200)

pacman::p_load(tidyverse, RcppRoll)

# Load all the functions for this question from the code folder
list.files("code/", full.names = TRUE) %>% .[grepl("[.]R$", .)] %>% walk(~source(.))

Funds <- Q3_Funds(read_rds("data/Active_Managers.rds"), read_rds("data/ABC_Fund.rds"))
Bench <- Q3_Bench(read_rds("data/Index_Returns_Daily.rds"))
Cash  <- Q3_Cash(read_rds("data/STeFI_Index.rds"))

Roll_Beta <- Q3_Rolling_Beta(Funds, Bench, Window = 36)
PCA       <- Q3_PCA(Funds, Months = 60)
Rank      <- Q3_Rolling_Rank(Funds, Window = 36)
Score     <- Q3_Scorecard(Funds, Bench, Cash)
Disp      <- Q3_Market_Dispersion(read_rds("data/Monthly_Index_Constituents.rds"), read_rds("data/Stock_Returns_Daily.rds"))
ABC_M     <- Q3_ABC_Monthly(Funds, Bench, Disp)
Alpha     <- Q3_Alpha(Funds, Bench, Cash)
PCA_F     <- Q3_PCA_Prac(Funds, Months = 60)
```

## ABC Fund in three points

- **Less market, more manager.** ABC's market beta is about half that of the typical peer, and a smaller share of its returns comes from the market than for 95% of peers.
- **Consistently strong.** Top-quartile on rolling 3-year returns 70% of the time since 2015, ahead of about 90% of peers on return, risk-adjusted return and drawdown, and an alpha higher than 98% of peers.
- **Protection when it counts.** In the market's worst months, ABC has lost on average about a third as much as the market (-1.7% vs -4.6%).

::: notes
The rest of the deck backs up each of these three points with the industry data.
:::

## How much of the industry is just market exposure?

::: notes
Beta measures how much a fund moves with the market: a beta of 1 means the fund rises and falls one-for-one with the Capped SWIX. Most active managers sit at 0.8-0.9, so most of what clients pay active fees for is market exposure they could get cheaply. ABC's beta has fallen steadily to about 0.4, roughly half the typical peer's.
:::

```{r beta-box}
Plot_Q3_Beta_Box(Q3_Beta_Snapshots(Roll_Beta))
```

## Does ABC offer something other than market beta?

::: notes
The vertical axis shows how much of each fund's monthly return is explained by the market. For most peers it is over 80%. For ABC it is about 40%, lower than for 95% of peers. The majority of ABC's return comes from its own decisions, not from the market.
:::

```{r beta-r2}
Plot_Q3_Beta_R2(Roll_Beta)
```

## What drives returns across the industry?

::: notes
Looking at all peer funds together, a single common driver (essentially the market) explains over 80% of how the whole industry's returns move. For the typical peer it explains close to 90% of returns; for ABC under 60%. In other words, most peers move as one herd, while ABC's returns are driven by different things, which is exactly what makes it useful in a client portfolio alongside other funds.
:::

```{r drivers}
Plot_Q3_Drivers(PCA)
```

## Relative performance over time

::: notes
The line shows where ABC ranks among peers on 3-year returns at each point in time. It has spent 70% of the time in the top quartile and was in the bottom quartile only briefly. The recent dip in 2025 should be acknowledged: in a strong, broad-based rally a lower-beta fund naturally lags, which is the other side of its protection in falling markets.
:::

```{r rank}
Plot_Q3_Rank(Rank)
```

## Scorecard against peers

::: notes
Since 2015 ABC has done better than about 9 out of 10 peers on every key measure: higher return, lower volatility, a better Sharpe ratio, a smaller worst loss and less market exposure. Delivering more return with less risk is rare among active managers.
:::

```{r scorecard}
Plot_Q3_Scorecard(Score)
```

## The dispersion argument: an honest check

::: notes
The claim that ABC does especially well when market dispersion is high is not supported by the data: its excess return is, if anything, slightly lower in high-dispersion months, and a formal test finds no relationship. It is better to avoid this claim with clients and use the message on the next slide, which the data strongly supports.
:::

```{r dispersion}
Plot_Q3_Dispersion(ABC_M)
```

## Where ABC really earns its place

::: notes
In the market's worst months, the Capped SWIX fell 4.6% on average and the typical peer 3.5%, but ABC only 1.7%. ABC gives up some upside in the very best months, but losing much less in bad months is what compounds into better long-run returns with lower risk. Only 1% of peers protect capital better in falling markets.
:::

```{r market-regimes}
Plot_Q3_Market_Regimes(ABC_M)
```

## Skill or luck?

::: notes
Alpha is the return a fund earned beyond what its market exposure explains. ABC's alpha of about 3.6% a year is higher than 98% of peers. The t-statistic measures how reliably that alpha was earned: above 2 means it is unlikely to be luck. Only 3% of peers clear that bar; ABC sits just below it (significant at the 10% level), so the evidence of skill is strong but should not be overstated. The typical peer's alpha is slightly negative.
:::

```{r alpha}
Plot_Q3_Alpha(Alpha)
```

## Why include ABC in client portfolios

- **A genuine diversifier:** most of its return comes from the manager's own decisions, not from the market or the industry herd.
- **Downside protection:** it loses far less than peers and the market when markets fall, which supports long-term compounding.
- **Proven over time:** strong peer rankings across most of the last decade on both return and risk, and an alpha of about 3.6% a year, one of the highest in the peer group.
- **Points to note:** ABC tends to lag in the strongest rallies (as in 2025), past performance does not guarantee future results, and benchmark comparisons start in 2015.

::: notes
Data notes: peer returns are winsorised each month at the 1st and 99th percentiles (one fund reports -55% in its final month before closing). Benchmark-based measures use the Capped SWIX from January 2015. Peers that closed during the period are included while they were active.
:::


## Technical appendix: principal component analysis

::: notes
For the more technical audience. The scree plot shows that one component explains about 82% of the variation in peer returns, with every other component explaining less than 4%. In the correlation circle, each grey arrow is a peer fund: almost all point to the edge of the circle along the first component, meaning they are almost entirely explained by it. ABC (added as a supplementary variable, so it does not influence the components) has a shorter arrow that points upwards, meaning less of its return is explained by the common driver and more by the secondary one.
:::

```{r pca-appendix}
Plot_Q3_PCA_Prac(PCA_F)
```
